title: Using TypeScript with Node.js
learning_outcomes: Describe JavaScript versus TypeScript responsibilities and explain how it relates to Using TypeScript with Node.js.
Demonstrate Type checking in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Compiler and runtime distinctions.

content.intro: Using TypeScript with Node.js is part of typescript and other runtime integrations. This lesson connects JavaScript versus TypeScript responsibilities, Type checking, Compiler and runtime distinctions to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: TypeScript and other runtime integrations are ecosystem choices whose execution and build requirements depend on the installed Node.js version and tooling. Use the documented compiler/runtime version, run its checks, and test the emitted or directly executed program.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: TypeScript and other runtime integrations are ecosystem choices whose execution and build requirements depend on the installed Node.js version and tooling. Treat TypeScript integration as optional and version-sensitive; separate type-checking/build steps from runtime assumptions.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Using TypeScript with Node.js. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with JavaScript versus TypeScript responsibilities; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Type checking, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every TypeScript feature, package condition, or loader works identically in every Node.js version.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the official Node.js TypeScript documentation and state exactly which workflow the project uses.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
